case_name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
subject: Arrest Guidelines & Checklists for Offences < 7 Years Imprisonment
principle: Police officers shall not automatically arrest accused when offence is punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Notice under Section 35(3) BNSS (formerly 41A CrPC) must be served. Arrest checklist must be furnished to Magistrate stating reasons why arrest was necessary.

case_name: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of Uttar Pradesh
subject: Mandatory Registration of FIR in Cognizable Offences
principle: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 173 BNSS (154 CrPC) if information discloses commission of a cognizable offence. Preliminary enquiry allowed only in matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence, or corruption cases, capped at statutory time limit.

case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
subject: Arrest and Custodial Rights Guidelines (Inspection Memo, Intimation to Relative)
principle: Mandates 11 fundamental guidelines: preparation of arrest memo signed by at least one witness/relative, right of accused to inform a friend/relative within 8-12 hours, mandatory medical examination upon arrest, and right to meet advocate during interrogation.

subject: Bail Guidelines and Categorization of Offences
principle: Categorized offences for uniform bail adjudication. Reiterated that investigation agencies must comply with Section 41A/Sec 35 BNSS. Strict action against investigating officers who violate procedural mandates.

case_name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
subject: Mandatory Certificate for Electronic Evidence Admissibility
principle: Production of certificate under Section 63 BSA (formerly 65B(4) IEA) is a condition precedent to the admissibility of electronic record by way of secondary evidence. If phone/hard disk is primary evidence in original state, certificate is not strictly necessary if seized properly.

case_name: State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya & Pulukuri Kottaya v. King-Emperor
subject: Discovery of Fact under Recovery Memo (Section 23 BSA)
principle: Only so much of information given by accused in police custody which relates distinctly to the discovery of a concealed fact/object is admissible in evidence. The weapon or property must be recovered exclusively upon the information of the accused.

case_name: Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh
subject: Mandatory Videography of Crime Scene & Seizure Process
principle: Recommended introducing videography and photography during crime scene investigation, seizure of mudamal, and body search to ensure credibility and transparency — now codified under Section 105 BNSS.

case_name: Joginder Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh
subject: Right to Counsel and Intimation of Arrest to Family
principle: No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so. The existence of the power to arrest is one thing; the justification for the exercise of it is quite another. Right of arrested person to have one friend, relative, or well-wisher informed of arrest — now mandated under Section 35 BNSS (D.K. Basu guidelines reinforced).

case_name: Rajesh Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh
subject: Safeguards Against Automatic Arrest in Section 498A (BNS Sec 85) Cases
principle: Directed constitution of Family Welfare Committees for preliminary scrutiny before arrest in dowry/cruelty cases. Reinforces Arnesh Kumar mandate for Section 35 BNSS notice. Arrest in BNS Section 85 (498A) cases requires Magistrate verification of preliminary inquiry report.

case_name: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat (Best Bakery Case)
subject: Fair Investigation and Witness Protection in Communal Violence Cases
principle: The right to fair trial encompasses fair investigation. In communal violence cases, trial must be shifted if local witness protection is compromised. IO has statutory duty to record all eyewitness accounts accurately and cannot selectively record statements. SC ordered re-investigation and transfer of case.

subject: Phone Tapping, Surveillance and Privacy Rights in Investigation
principle: Telephone tapping constitutes a serious invasion of the individual's privacy and is only permissible under strict procedural safeguards. An order for phone surveillance requires Home Secretary's approval, stated reasons, and review committees. Any evidence gathered in violation of these safeguards may be challenged under BSA.

case_name: Ritesh Sinha v. State of Uttar Pradesh
subject: Voice Sample of Accused Under Investigation
principle: A magistrate has the power to order an accused to give a voice sample for comparison with recorded voice during investigation. This does not violate Article 20(3) (right against self-incrimination). Voice samples stored as electronic records are admissible under Section 61 BSA if authenticated properly.

case_name: State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad
subject: Handwriting Samples, Fingerprints and Specimen Evidence Not Self-Incrimination
principle: Compelling an accused to give handwriting samples, fingerprints, footprints, blood samples, or photographs does not amount to self-incrimination under Article 20(3). Such specimen evidence is physical evidence, not a testimonial act, and its collection is mandated under Section 53 BNSS by a Medical Practitioner.
